I’ve never seen this particularly well addressed with land value taxation, but how is it compatible with and how does it interface with zoning? If zoning is too restrictive, then the value of land value taxation is inherently not going to be fully realised and the whole point of implementing it is kind of moot. 

It then runs into some other issues, namely determining what constitutes “unimproved land” or “optimal use”. How does land value taxation account for counterintuitive or irrational existing or future outcomes? For instance, a place like a historic arts district in a major metropolis derives much of its value from its architecture and design, but no one would say that its land use and form is fully “built-out” since its mostly mid-rise. 

A few other issues comes to mind, namely longer-term strategic spatial planning. The nature  of land value taxation is inherently is conflicting here: does the owner of the property develop it to the maximum value that’s existing or potential in the future? If the former, then that could be incompatible with longer-term needs for expected population growth since there are viability issues financially (based on current or very near-term needs). We see this problem a lot with unit mixes: there may be strategic reasons why a municipality wants to encourage more family-sized units rather than studios, but the math for a land value tax may not allow that to work out. If the latter, then how does land value taxation address the need to phase development and coordinate it with associated infrastructure?

Maybe I’m totally wrong here but it’s always struck me as a great theoretical concept but I have no clue how you handle it in practice. There are too many conflicting interests and goals.

I think the problem is that in urban planning, there are tons of cases where the market and locality have contrasting or competing interests and the scale of this misalignment and need for zoning or regulations for a slew of issues (transportation and infrastructure provision, environmental protection, form-based attributes, the need to maintain distance or separation of specific uses such as industrial or logistics from residential to name a few) that the conditions for LVT to work can’t exist in practice. 

Similarly, planning departments have to manage and coordinate multiple actors and parties. I brought up the point about current or future use because the current setup means that the two are, to a large degree, interlinked. Planning guidance provides all parties - public bodies, developers and residents - with a framework for understanding typically a two-decade timeframe for land use policy and outcomes. Within that there’s scope for variation, but generally speaking it enables a degree of contextual consistency that’s needed for being able to plan things like school space requirements, utility provisions and other aspects of municipal management outside of the realm or purview of developers. Absent that, we would likely end up with wildly variant land use that is often less efficient.

But again (and maybe I didn't articulate this point well enough), this is an overly simplistic way of thinking about the practicalities of land use because it doesn't take into account the inherent variation in value as well as contextual, strategic and spatial needs beyond that of the owner of the land. That is: not all land is of equal value and, more importantly, the maximum efficiency of a parcel in isolation is not necessarily in the best interest of the wider community or region. This is because there are complementary considerations that are the responsibility of other public bodies or private actors. LVT treats all land as being theoretically equal at a baseline because the same rate of tax is assessed on it to start, but that's a flawed premise.

No worries. I have a background in urban planning and work in a tangential field so it’s something I think about all the time. 

Which issues exactly are you referencing here? Just how planning currently handles the need to balance development and future use? It obviously depends on the national and local frameworks and what they allow, but generally speaking we start with a framework with a broad goal of an “outcome” in terms of scale, scope, grain and connectivity, both within the target geography and to the broader area. From there, we then layer on more specific requirements. These can range from density requirements to bulk controls to unit mix profiles to affordability mandates. 

Not all will necessarily show up and there’s a lot more in there, but generally this allows the public body in charge of planning to come up with a broad estimate of how the area will grow in the future and from there how other departments will need to allocate resources for expanding associated infrastructure. This also provides guidance for investors and developers to have a sense of what types of schemes will be possible and they can make a determination of viability. Parties of local interest can also figure out to some degree what their community will look and feel like moving forward and this helps with longer-term planning. Basically, strategic guidance better articulates and identifies up front what inefficiencies will need to be accounted for and explains why they need to be considered. 

Re: my comment, I’m saying essentially that LVT’s underlying concept is that the owner of the land is best served by maximising the amount of improvement or development that can take place. This is intuitively logical, but only in isolation. The need to accommodate and balance myriad interests and outcomes often means overriding the highest and best use of the land on its own. A good example would be if you were in a fast-growing city with a lot of demand for office. A developer might say that planting an office building somewhere could grant an easy return, but if there’s a lot of inbound movement then the incorrect placement of this type of use could result in a lack of transit accessibility, inability to later improve connectivity and links to the site and lead to dispersion rather than clustering. In this case, the negative outcomes of leaving the decision of how to develop the land to the owner outweigh what might be - at the time - the fastest way to “improve” it.
